text: The light oil deposits of the world are depleting, which has generated a need to better understand the chemical composition of crude oil of different geographical origins. Specifically, for chemically enhanced oil recovery processes, this information would enable producers to investigate the phase and interfacial interactions between oil, surfactants, and reservoir rock, and thereby help the industry develop smarter, more efficient solutions for the economic recovery of oil [1] [2] [3] . Further, the ability to obtain an accurate estimate of the average molecular weight of crude oil would facilitate the optimization of refinery processes [4] . This is especially important for conversion of crude oil via reactions such as alkylation, dimerization, cracking, and hydrotreating, since access to an accurate average molecular weight would enable a better estimation of the amount of reagent required for the conversion [4] . The challenge of analyzing crude oil is that it is a complex mixture, predicted to contain as many or more compounds than the number of genes in the human genome [5] . To study such complex mixtures, powerful high-resolution mass spectrometers, such as Fourier-transform ion cyclotron resonance or orbitrap mass spectrometers, are desirable [6, 7] . These high-resolution instruments can be used to determine the elemental compositions of ionized crude oil components, which facilitates categorizing them into different compound classes (such the hydrocarbon class containing only carbon and hydrogen and heteroatom classes containing oxygen, nitrogen and/or sulfur in addition to carbon and hydrogen) or compound types (e.g., saturated and aromatic compounds). While the information provided by these techniques is invaluable, problems associated with the ionization methods employed include inefficient ionization, competition for ionization, and matrix effects, all of which may reduce sensitivity toward or even entirely prevent the detection of some components of crude oil. Indeed, most of these studies have employed atmospheric pressure chemical ionization (APCI) for nonpolar analytes [8] , atmospheric pressure photo ionization (APPI) for aromatic analytes [7, 9] and electrospray ionization (ESI) for polar analytes [10, 11] . Unfortunately, all these methods selectively ionize only some of the crude oil components. Above problems of competition for ionization and matrix effects are reduced when the mass analysis is preceded by a chromatographic separation [12] [13] [14] .

Chromatography reduces the complexity of the mixture by separating it into fractions, but it does not necessarily eliminate issues having to do with mixture components with widely differing ionization efficiencies. In this paper, a new separation and characterization method for crude oil is introduced, entitled Distillation Precipitation Fractionation Mass Spectrometry (DPF-MS). DPF-MS involves separation of the crude oil into several fractions that contain compounds with similar chemical characteristics, followed by molecular level characterization of each fraction by using an optimized mass spectrometric method. The novelty of this method lies in the optimization of the ionization and mass spectrometry method separately for each fraction by using representative model compounds so that all compounds in each fraction are ionized at approximately the same efficiency to yield stable ionized molecules, which makes the DPF-MS method semi-quantitative. Following the weighing and analysis of each fraction, consideration of mass balance facilitated the molecular profiling of the fractionated crude oil.

text: Crude oil was separated into six fractions by using different techniques. As a first step, the most volatile compounds in the crude oil were separated by vacuum distillation at room temperature to yield fraction I (distillate) to avoid their loss during fractionation. The remaining residue was separated into asphaltenes (fraction II) and maltenes (all remaining fractions) through precipitation of the asphaltenes by using hexane as reported in the literature [15] . Maltenes were further chromatographically separated into three fractions (C 6 H 14 -eluted fractions III and IV combined, CH 2 Cl 2 -eluted fraction V, and i-C 3 H 7 OHeluted fraction VI) on an auto column (Combi-flash Rf 200 from Teledyne Isco, Inc.) by using hexane (C 6 H 14 ), dichloromethane (CH 2 Cl 2 ) and isopropanol (i-C 3 H 7 OH) as eluents. The C 6 H 14 -eluted fractions were further separated into fractions III and IV by using a solid phase extraction technique reported in the literature [16, 17] . Further details of each separation step are provided in the Supporting information (Table S2 ). All the fractions were weighted gravimetrically to obtain mass balance and recovery.

text: A LECO Pegasus 4D GCxGC/(EI)TOF instrument equipped with an Agilent 7890B two-dimensional gas chromatograph (Agilent technologies, Santa Clara, CA) and a high-resolution time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectrometer (up to 50,000 resolution) was used for the analysis of the volatile compounds (fraction I) in crude oil. After separation of the compounds, positive ion mode electron ionization (EI) (70 eV) was used to ionize the compounds upon entrance into the mass spectrometer. The EI mass spectra measured (at high resolution) for unknown compounds were compared to extensive EI mass spectral libraries for identification (NIST libraries). This analysis yielded a list of identified compounds, their gas chromatographic peak areas and two retention times, and their chemical formulas and chemical classes. Experimental conditions are detailed in the Supporting information (Table S3 ). Additionally, GCxGC/(EI)TOF was used to optimize the solid phase extraction parameters for optimal separation of the C 6 H 14 -eluted fraction III from IV. The efficiency of solid phase extraction was evaluated by monitoring the percentage of coelution or carryover of different chemical classes of compounds into the separated fractions. Experimental conditions are detailed in Supporting information (Table S4 ).

text: Positive ion mode atmospheric pressure ionization methods using different nebulizing gases and solvents, such as APPI/N 2 /CS 2 , APCI/N 2 / CS 2 , APCI/O 2 /n-hexane, APCI/N 2 /n-hexane, APCI/N 2 /n-hexane and methanol, APCI/N 2 /toluene, APCI/N 2 /methanol, and ESI/N 2 /methanol, were tested for specific fractions (II, III, IV, V and VI). Three different APCI techniques were identified to be most effective for these five fractions. APCI/N 2 /CS 2 was selected for the analysis of fractions II, IV, and V, APCI/O 2 /n-hexane for fraction III, and APCI/N 2 /n-hexane and methanol for fraction VI. The optimized parameters used for the ionization of compounds in these fractions are summarized in Table S5 . Xcaliber version 2.2 (Thermo Fischer Scientific, Inc, San Jose, CA) was used for data acquisition and analysis. The normalized peak height threshold for peak picking was 5%. After peak picking, elemental formulas were assigned based on accurately measured m/z values that were within 3 ppm from the theoretical value (accepted mass accuracy with external calibration). Elements used for formula assignments were carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, oxygen and sulfur. While no limits were placed on the number of carbons and hydrogens used for the elemental composition assignment, limits of 4 nitrogen, 5 oxygen, and 5 sulfur atoms were used. The degree of unsaturation, also known as ring and double bond (RDB) equivalent, represents the number of rings plus the number of double bonds in a molecule. This value was calculated based on the assigned elemental composition by using Eq. ( S1 ) provided in the supporting information. Data sorting for plotting the graphs and heteroatom classification was performed using Excel. RDB equivalent versus carbon number plots and heteroatom distribution plots were prepared by using OriginPro (version 93E).

text: FTIR measurements were performed on all the separated crude oil fractions with a Nicolet 6700 FTIR spectrometer (Thermo Scientific). The FTIR spectra were collected using a liquid N 2 cooled MCT (HgCdTe) detector. The scans involved wave numbers from 4000 up to 650 cm -1 with a resolution of 2 cm -1 and 64 scans co-added per sample. The spectrum of each fraction was corrected against the background spectrum obtained by using the clean, dry cell. Attenuated total reflectance (ATR-FTIR) measurements were made using two different methods. For liquid fractions with sufficient volume of 0.5 mL, a 10-bounce horizontal ATR cell (Pike Technologies, Madison, WI) was used. The internal reflection element (IRE) used was a ZnSe crystal with dimensions of 73 mm by 7 mm and an angle of incidence of 45°. The total volume of the cell was 2 mL. For viscous fractions or semi-solid materials (e.g., asphaltenes), a single bounce diamond ATR cell (GladiATR™ Pike Technologies) was used.

text: In order to illustrate some of the problems associated with detection of all compounds in crude oil by mass spectrometry without prior separation, a simple equimolar mixture containing typical crude oil components, i.e., two alkylaromatic compounds (n-decylbenzene, nhexylbenzene), an alkane (pentadecane), two cycloalkanes (cycloheptane, methylcyclopentane), an alkene (1-decene) and an alkyne (1hexyne), was analyzed by using APCI and APPI. This mixture cannot be ionized using the traditional APCI and APPI solvent systems, water and/or methanol, as the hydrocarbons are not soluble in these solvents. Carbon disulfide (CS 2 ) has been successfully used in the past as a solvent for APCI of hydrocarbon mixtures [8] . Therefore, the model compound mixture was dissolved in CS 2 and analyzed by using both APCI/N 2 /CS 2 (N 2 was used as the nebulizing gas) and APPI/N 2 /CS 2 ionization methods in a LQIT-orbitrap MS. Fig. 1 shows the APCI/N 2 / CS 2 mass spectrum of the model mixture. Compounds in this mixture were also analyzed individually by using APCI/N 2 /CS 2 to identify the ions (fragment ions and intact molecular ions) produced by each individual compound. The linear alkane fragmented completely upon ionization, generating fragment ions of m/ z 57, 71 and 85 and no visible molecular ions, which makes detection of this alkane challenging. The alkyne generated stable molecular ions as well as minor fragment ions of m/z 67. The alkene also produced both stable molecular ions as well as fragment ions of m/z 57 and 70. However, the fragmentation was extensive, with some fragment ions having an equal abundance as the molecular ions. The alkylaromatic compounds were observed to generate mostly stable molecular ions, with minimal fragmentation to form ions of m/z 92. The cycloalkanes generated stable molecular ions, molecular ions that had lost a hydrogen atom and fragment ions of m/z 56, which complicates data analysis. The APPI/N 2 /CS 2 method produced similar results (Fig. S1 in the supporting information). In conclusion, the mass spectrum shows more fragment ions than molecular ions, and the molecular ions of different compounds have widely differing relative abundances. Some molecular ions fragment only to a small extent while others have extensive fragmentation.

text: Distillation, precipitation, autocolumn fractionation and solid phase extraction were used to separate the compounds in the crude oil into six fractions based on their differences in volatility, solubility and polarity. A schematic for the complete separation process is presented in Fig. 2 . As the first step, the most volatile compounds in the crude oil were separated by room-temperature vacuum distillation from the nonvolatile portion (residue) to generate fraction 1. During distillation, the receiving flask was kept at a low temperature by using dry ice and acetone (< -70 °C) to collect and condense the volatile components. The remaining residue was separated into asphaltenes (fraction II) and maltenes (all remaining fractions) through precipitation of the asphaltenes by using n-hexane as described in literature [15] . Maltenes were chromatographically separated into three fractions (n-hexane-eluted fraction (corresponding to fractions III and IV) and fractions V and VI) based on their differences in polarity. This separation was accomplished by using an auto column coupled with evaporative light scattering (ELSD) and UV detectors and the eluents n-hexane (n-C 6 H 14 ), dichloromethane (CH 2 Cl 2 ) and isopropanol (i-C 3 H 7 OH), used in this order. Fig. 3 shows a typical auto column chromatogram of maltenes. The presence of both ELSD and UV signals in the later eluting part of the hexane-eluted fraction (Fig. 3 ) indicated co-elution of two different analyte classes, aliphatic (no UV absorption) and aromatic hydrocarbons (UV absorption). To test this hypothesis, this fraction was analyzed using GCxGC/(EI)TOF MS. Indeed, based on the total ion current GC/GC chromatogram (Fig. S2A in supporting information), the n-C 6 H 14 -eluted fraction is a co-eluted mixture of heavy saturated (cyclic, linear and branched) and light aromatic hydrocarbons. Therefore, an additional separation step was necessary. The saturated and aromatic hydrocarbon classes in the n-hexane-eluted fraction were separated via solid phase extraction to produce fractions III (heavy saturated hydrocarbons) and IV (light aromatic hydrocarbons), thus increasing the total number of maltene fractions from three to four (the last two being fractions V and VI eluted by dichloromethane and isopropanol, respectively). The success of the solid phase extraction was evaluated by using GCxGC/(EI)TOF MS to analyze fraction III (Fig. S2B in supporting information).

text: Based on the FTIR results, the distillate (fraction I) contains saturated hydrocarbons. As this fraction is volatile, the compounds were separated and analyzed using GCxGC/electron ionization (EI) high-resolution time-of-flight (TOF) MS. EI is a universal ionization method (able to ionize all organic compounds) and it provides library-searchable, highly reproducible mass spectra, which allowed for identification of many of the compounds. The suitability of this method for the semiquantitative analysis of volatile saturated hydrocarbons has been evaluated earlier by using model compound mixtures [18] . The most abundant compounds identified in this fraction are alkanes and cycloalkanes containing 7-10 carbons. The full list of compounds identified is provided in Section VI of supporting information. The remaining five nonvolatile fractions were analyzed using methods other than GCxGC/MS as this method can be reliably used only for relatively volatile compounds. FTIR spectral analysis of fractions II (asphaltenes), IV (light aromatic compounds) and V (heteroaromatic compounds) revealed the presence of predominantly aromatic compounds. The APCI/N 2 /CS 2 method is well suited for the ionization of these types of compounds as it has been reported [8] to ionize different types of aromatic analytes at nearly equal efficiency by predominant formation of stable molecular ions without substantial fragmentation (see Fig. S4 in supporting information for confirmation of this finding by using a model compound mixture). Therefore, compounds in the fractions II, IV and V were ionized by using this method. Other ionization methods, such as APCI/N 2 /toluene and APCI/N 2 /methanol, were also examined. However, they were found to be less successful than the APCI/N 2 /CS 2 ionization method (see Fig. S5 in supporting information). Though APCI/N 2 /CS 2 method has been demonstrated to be successful in ionizing polyaromatic model compounds with long alkyl chains without substantial fragmentation [8] , ionization of monoaromatic model compounds with long alkyl chains (n-phenyldecane, n-phenyldodecane and n-heptadecylbenzene) was observed here to result in the formation of a fragment ion of m/z 92 (toluene radical cation) (see Fig. S6 in supporting information). All three compounds studied generate this fragment ion.

text: In order to test the accuracy of the optimized mass spectrometry methods discussed above for the determination of the average molecular weights (Avg MW) of the crude oil fractions and ultimately the crude oil itself, the experimental Avg MW was determined for the four model compound mixtures discussed above by using the optimized methods (Table S7 ). text: Assigning accurate elemental compositions for ionized compounds is critical for the accurate estimation of compound class distributions. However, when analyzing mixtures as complex as crude oil, this requires much greater resolution and mass accuracy than available on the orbitrap (100,000 resolution) and TOF instruments (50,000 resolution) used in this research [21] [22] [23] [24] . However, after DPF separation of the crude oil into six fractions based on the volatility, solubility and polarity of the compounds, much simpler mixtures are generated and the compounds in each mixture have similar properties. This makes assigning elemental compositions much easier when using lower resolution instruments. Elemental composition data thus obtained for ionized compounds derived from the different crude oil fractions can be utilized to further classify the compounds into different compound classes. Fig. 9 (Table S8 ) shows compound class distributions and their relative abundances for the six fractions. The percentage relative abundance of the hydrocarbon (HC) class was found to be different for each fraction, being the greatest for the distillate (fraction I) and the smallest for the polar compounds (fraction VI). The asphaltenes (fraction II) contain a relatively large number of compounds with a variety of different heteroatoms. While N atoms and SO 3 groups were most abundant in heteroaromatic compounds (fraction V), SO, O and SO 4 atoms/groups are most abundant in polar compounds (fraction VI). Interestingly, some compounds in the aromatic hydrocarbon fraction were found to contain not only S but also NS 2 . To summarize, all the fractions are drastically different in their compound class distributions and their relative abundances. From the gravimetric weight percentage of individual fractions and their compound class distributions, the weight percentage distribution of individual compound classes in the whole crude oil can be obtained by using Eq. (S7). Fig. 10 (Table S8 ) shows the summarized weight percentage distributions for the different compound classes consolidated from the data obtained for the individual fractions. These data provide a simplified picture on the presence of different compound classes and their abundances in the whole crude oil. Based on these consolidated results, this crude oil consists of about 12% sulfur containing compounds (S, OS and O 3 S). It can also be deduced that this crude oil is very low (3%) in oxygen content (O, O 3 and O 4 ).

Further information on individual fractions can be obtained by exploiting the tandem MS capabilities of the LQIT/orbitrap mass spectrometer. This mass spectrometer allows the isolation of a group of isomeric and isobaric ions of a given m/z-value followed by collisionactivated dissociation (CAD) in the ion trap. The resulting MS/MS CAD spectra can provide structural information on crude oil components, such as the number of carbons in alkyl groups and the size of the aromatic cores in asphaltenes [25, 26] . text: A separation and characterization method entitled Distillation Precipitation Fractionation Mass Spectrometry (DPF-MS) is introduced here for the analysis of crude oil at the molecular level. This method involves separation of the crude oil into six fractions. These fractions are the distillate (fraction I) mostly containing volatile saturated hydrocarbons but also light aromatic hydrocarbons, asphaltenes (fraction II) containing predominantly aromatic and heteroaromatic compounds, heavy saturated hydrocarbons (fraction III) containing cyclic, branched and linear hydrocarbons, aromatic hydrocarbons (fraction III) containing predominantly alkylaromatic compounds, heteroaromatic compounds (fraction V) containing mostly aromatic compounds, and polar compounds (fraction VI) containing nonaromatic polar compounds. High-resolution mass spectrometry instruments, specifically, GCxGC/TOF and LQIT/orbitrap mass spectrometers, were used for the molecular level characterization of each individual fraction. An optimized ionization method was developed for each fraction to ionize all of its components with similar efficiency and to generate only one type of ions, either molecular ions, protonated molecules or cations formed upon hydride abstraction. While (+) EI ionization method coupled with GCxGC/TOF was utilized for the characterization of the volatile distillate (fraction I), (+) APCI approaches with different nebulization gases and solvent systems were used for each nonvolatile fraction (fractions II, III, IV, V, VI). DPF-MS provides semi-quantitative molecular level information (elemental compositions and molecular weights) that can be further processed to obtain accurate average molecular weight, ring and double bond equivalence values and percentage abundances of different compound classes in the different crude oil fractions. This method excels over previous methods by including the mass balance for each fraction, thus allowing for data consolidation (data obtained from different fractions consolidated into one data set), which provides an accurate overall analysis of the crude oil, including average molecular weight, heteroatom content, and weight percentage of different compound classes.

text: Over the past decades, the quality of crude oil recovered from oil wells has been declining because much of the light crude oil has been already removed from the reservoirs, leaving behind heavier crude oil [1] [2] [3] . Unfortunately, heavier crude oil has a lower value because it is more difficult to process [4] . The formal classification of crude oil as heavy or light is based on the American Petroleum Institute (API) gravity, which is a measure for the density of the crude oil relative to water [5] . This value is commonly determined by using a reference method detailed in the ASTM D4052 document [6] . Crude oil classified as heavy has an API gravity lower than 22.3 while medium and light crude oils have API gravities between 22.3 and 31.1 and equal to or > 31.1, respectively [7] . Although API gravity is a generally accepted tool for classifying crude oils, some crude oils with the same API gravity exhibit different physical properties (such as viscosity) [8] , suggesting that these crude oils have different chemical compositions and therefore probably also different chemical properties. A more accurate way to classify crude oils needs to be developed. The first step in this direction is to establish correlations between the chemical composition of crude oils and their selected physical properties, such as API gravity. Although mass spectrometry provides a powerful tool for the compositional analysis of crude oil [9] [10] [11] , it has limitations. For example, no single ionization method, with the exception of electron ionization, ionizes efficiently all the different compound types in crude oil [12] . Unfortunately, electron ionization causes extensive fragmentation to saturated hydrocarbons, which complicates the analysis of these very complex mixtures. All other ionization methods have a bias for only certain types of analytes. For example, electrospray ionization (ESI) operated in positive ion mode selectively ionizes the most basic compounds in a mixture, and therefore provides an inaccurate representation of the chemical compositions of crude oil samples as most compounds in crude oil are not basic [13] . In spite of their limitations, mass spectrometric methods have been used to explore correlations between API gravity and chemical compositions of crude oils.

text: For example, electrospray ionization (ESI) operated in positive ion mode selectively ionizes the most basic compounds in a mixture, and therefore provides an inaccurate representation of the chemical compositions of crude oil samples as most compounds in crude oil are not basic [13] . In spite of their limitations, mass spectrometric methods have been used to explore correlations between API gravity and chemical compositions of crude oils. For example, examination of the amounts of aromatic compounds in twenty crude oils has demonstrated a correlation between the API gravity of a crude oil and the concentrations of aromatic compounds containing one nitrogen atom or one nitrogen and one oxygen atom, as determined by using (+) atmospheric pressure photoionization (APPI) with toluene dopant coupled to Fourier-transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS) [14] . However, only a weak correlation was found for the API gravity and the total nitrogen mass percent determined by direct elemental analysis (correlation coefficient R 2 = 0.5) for the same crude oils. This discrepancy may be due to a limited ability of the APPI method to detect nonaromatic nitrogen-compounds. In other studies, the crude oil samples were subjected to SARA fractionation before MS analysis. SARA involves separating crude oils into four fractions. First, asphaltenes are precipitated. After this, the remaining compounds (maltenes) are chromatographically separated to obtain four fractions referred to as asphaltenes, saturated compounds, aromatic compounds, and resins [15, 16] . In one such study, a correlation was found between the API gravity of three crude oils and the average ring and double bond equivalence (RDBE; related to the level of unsaturation and number of rings) of compounds containing one nitrogen atom in the resin and asphaltene fractions [7] . The average RDBE was determined using (+) ESI FT-ICR MS; therefore, only basic compounds were detected in this study. In another study, SARA fractionation of five heavy crude oils followed by thermal analysis coupled with (+) atmospheric pressure chemical ionization (APCI) FT-ICR MS revealed that the API gravity was inversely related to the average RDBE for compounds in the aromatic compound fraction [17] . However, it should be noted that the fractions obtained by SARA are still complex mixtures of compounds and not separate chemical classes. For example, the SARA fraction referred to as saturated compounds contains a substantial amount of aromatic compounds [18] .

Previously, we have demonstrated the benefits of a new approach referred to as Distillation, Precipitation, Fractionation Mass Spectrometry (DPF MS) for molecular profiling of crude oils [18] . This method involves fractionating crude oil into six major classes of compounds: volatile saturated hydrocarbons, asphaltenes, heavy saturated hydrocarbons, alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons, heteroaromatic compounds, and polar compounds. Optimized ionization and mass spectrometric analysis methods are then utilized for the analysis of each class. By utilizing a different ionization method and/or solvent, or solvent system, for each compound class, compounds within the class are ionized with similar efficiencies and with minimal fragmentation [18] . This method has been shown to enable the accurate determination of the chemical compositions of crude oils. In this study, the DPF MS method was utilized to characterize the molecular compositions of light, medium, and heavy crude oils in an attempt to find correlations between the chemical compositions and the API gravities of these samples.

text: Each of the five crude oil samples was fractionated according to the DPF method [18] into the six chemical classes mentioned above. The text volatile saturated hydrocarbon class was obtained by using vacuum distillation at room temperature. During vacuum distillation, a rough pump was used to generate a vacuum at the inlet of a receiving flask, which was connected to the distillation flask via a condenser. The condenser was cooled using cold water and the receiving flask was kept at a low temperature by using dry ice and acetone (< -70 °C) to collect and condense the volatile compounds. The remaining crude oil was weighed and subjected to precipitation of asphaltenes, as described previously [20] . The precipitated material was filtered with a 0.45 μm Whatman PTFE membrane filter, dried, and weighed. The remaining residue, referred to as maltenes, was chromatographically separated into three classes based on the polarity of the compounds by using different solvents in a Combi-flash Rf 200 auto column system (Teledyne Isco, Inc). A hexane-eluted fraction contained both heavy saturated hydrocarbon and alkyl aromatic hydrocarbon classes, while dichloromethane and isopropanol fractions contained the heteroaromatic compound and polar compound classes, respectively. The hexane fraction was further separated into heavy saturated hydrocarbon and alkyl aromatic hydrocarbon classes by using solid phase extraction with a Si/CN-S-1.5 g cartridge (Interchim).

text: A Mitsubishi Model TS-100 trace sulfur/nitrogen analyzer (Mitsubishi Chemical Corporation) was used to determine the total nitrogen content of each crude oil. Each sample was placed in a furnace kept at 800-1000 °C where nitrogen was oxidized to nitric oxide (NO) in an oxygen atmosphere. The NO was converted to excited nitrogen dioxide (NO 2 ) by ozone in the furnace. An inert sweep gas, argon, was used to move NO 2 to the detector. As the excited NO 2 decayed, the light emitted was detected by a chemiluminescence detector, a photomultiplier tube. This procedure followed the ASTM D5762 standard method [21] and was completed in duplicate measurements.

text: All compound classes were analyzed separately, as described previously [18] . With the exception of the volatile saturated hydrocarbons, all compound classes were analyzed using a Thermo Scientific linear quadrupole ion trap with a high-resolution orbitrap detector (LQIT/ orbitrap) equipped with APCI. Hexane was used as the solvent and the APCI reagent and oxygen was used as the sheath and auxiliary gas ((+) APCI/O 2 /hexane) for the heavy saturated hydrocarbon class. Oxygen was employed in place of the more commonly used nitrogen because linear saturated hydrocarbons produce [M] +• as well as [M-H] + ions and undergo extensive fragmentation when nitrogen was employed whereas only [M-H] + ions were produced when oxygen was used [22] . Aromatic hydrocarbon and heteroaromatic compound classes were analyzed with (+) APCI with carbon disulfide (CS 2 ) as the solvent and APCI reagent and nitrogen as the sheath and auxiliary gas ((+) APCI/N 2 /CS 2 ). The polar compound class was analyzed using (+) APCI with a 3:1 methanol:hexane solution as the solvent and APCI reagent and nitrogen as the sheath and auxiliary gas ((+) APCI/N 2 /3:1 methanol:hexane). Typical APCI conditions were as follows: the vaporizer temperature 300 °C, the transfer capillary temperature 275 °C, the sheath and auxiliary gas flow rates 30 and 10 arbitrary units, respectively, the discharge current 3.8 μA, and the transfer capillary and the tube lens voltages 10 and 40 V, respectively. Each compound class was dissolved in a preselected solvent or solvent system at a concentration of 30 mg/mL and directly infused into the APCI source at a flow rate of 10 μL/min. Compounds in the heteroaromatic compound class were further investigated by using in-source collision-activated dissociation (ISCAD) to cleave off alkyl chains from the aromatic cores in the ionized compounds. In these experiments, 100 V was applied to the multipoles and the lenses of the ion optics between the ion source and the linear quadrupole ion trap to accelerate all ions formed in the ion source. The accelerated ions collided with atoms and molecules in this region and dissociated. ISCAD can be used to cleave all alkyl side chains from alkyl aromatic ions [23, 24] .

An auto injector (Agilent G4513A) was used to inject 0.5 μL of the compound class into a split/splitless injector with a split ratio of 1:20 held at 260 °C at a constant flow of ultra-pure helium carrier gas (1.25 mL/min). text: A quad-jet dual stage thermal modulator was placed between the two columns. The modulator consisted of two hot jets and two cold jets, one hot and cold jet pair for stage one and one hot and cold jet pair for stage two. It used liquid nitrogen for cooling the cold jets and heated nitrogen gas for the hot jets. The total modulation time was 3.5 s. It was split between the two stages (1.75 s each), 0.6 s of which was used for the hot jet pulse and 1.15 s for the cold jet pulse. The modulator hot jet was offset by +80 °C from the temperature of the secondary oven containing the nonpolar column. The secondary oven was offset by +10 °C from the temperature of the primary oven and subjected to the same temperature program as the primary oven: heated to 45 °C and held there for 1 min after sample injection, heated to 65 °C at the rate of 1 °C/min, followed by heating to a maximum temperature of 185 °C at the rate of 3 °C/min, where it was held for 3 min. The transfer line between GC × GC and MS was held at 300 °C throughout the analysis. The MS ion source was heated to 250 °C. The eluted compounds were ionized by electron ionization (EI) using 70 eV electron kinetic energy and all ions were transferred into a TOF MS for high-resolution analysis (25,000 resolution at m/z 219). Mass spectra were collected at an acquisition rate of 200 Hz. Daily mass calibration and tuning were performed using perfluorotributylamine (PFTBA) as the calibrant. An acquisition delay of 300 s was employed to prevent the ionization of solvent, which would have saturated the detector and potentially harmed the EI filament. Data were collected over a m/z range of 45-550. Data collection, processing, and analysis were performed via a LECO Visual Basic Scripting (VBS) software, ChromaTOF version 5.10.58.0.52262. Wiley (2011) and NIST (2011) mass spectral databases were used for compound identification with a match factor threshold of > 800.

text: The Distillation, Precipitation, Fractionation Mass Spectrometry (DPF MS) approach [18] was used for molecular profiling of five crude oils with different API gravities. This method involves fractionating crude oil into six major classes of compounds: volatile saturated hydrocarbons, asphaltenes, heavy saturated hydrocarbons, alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons, heteroaromatic compounds, and polar compounds. Optimized ionization and mass spectrometric analysis methods are then utilized for the characterization of each compound class. Two different mass spectrometry methods were employed: a high-resolution two-dimensional gas chromatograph coupled with electron ionization/highresolution time-of-flight mass spectrometer (GC × GC/(EI) TOF MS) and an atmospheric pressure chemical ionization/linear quadrupole ion trap mass spectrometer coupled with a high-resolution orbitrap mass analyzer/detector ((APCI) LQIT/orbitrap). Correlations between the chemical compositions of the crude oil samples and their API gravity are discussed below, starting with correlations found for the crude oils as a whole, followed by correlations found for the individual compound classes.

text: The five crude oils were fractionated via the DPF methodology [18] to determine the gravimetric weight percent (wt%) of each compound class. In general, the heavier crude oils were found to contain more asphaltenes and heteroaromatic compounds and less heavy, alkyl aromatic and volatile saturated hydrocarbons than the lighter crude oils (Table 1 ). The heaviest crude oil contained substantially more polar compounds than the other crude oils and it contained no volatile saturated hydrocarbons. The only correlation found for API gravity and the gravimetric weight percents of the compound classes, based on Table 1 , was for the heteroaromatic compound class. As the weight percent of compounds in the heteroaromatic compound class increases, the API gravity decreases (R 2 = 0.931; Fig. S1 ). To obtain information on the elemental compositions of the compounds in the crude oils, each compound class was analyzed via a predetermined ionization and high-resolution mass spectrometric analysis method (results obtained for the different classes are discussed later) and the elemental compositions measured for each chemical class were consolidated using the measured total ion abundance of each chemical class and the gravimetric percentage of that class (wt %(x)), as shown in Eq. ( 3 ). This equation is based on the assumptions that the compounds in each compound class are ionized with similar efficiencies and with minimal fragmentation, which has been demonstrated to be true based on studies of model compound mixtures [18] . where i is the specific elemental composition of an ionized compound and x is the number of the compound class (1-6), ∑ x abundance is the total ion abundance measured for each compound class, and wt % (x) is the gravimetric percentage of each compound class. The consolidated elemental compositions revealed the lowest hydrocarbon (C c H h ) content for the heaviest crude oil and the greatest for the three lightest crude oils (Table 2 ). On the other hand, the heaviest crude oil appears to contain much greater amounts of compounds with the C c H h N (the most abundant N-containing compounds), C c H h N 2 and C c H h N 2 S 2 elemental compositions than the other crude oils. Further, compounds with the elemental composition C c H h O o were most abundant (17%) in the lightest crude oil.

text: In addition to consideration of the crude oils as a whole, the molecular compositions of the individual compound classes were compared for the different crude oils. The ionized compounds with different elemental compositions and their relative mass spectrometric abundances are shown in Tables S1-S6 . While no correlations were found between the API gravity and the weight percentages of compounds with different elemental compositions for the crude oils as a whole (Table 2 ), nor between the API gravity and the total nitrogen content (Table 3 ), as discussed above, this was not true when the compound classes were considered separately. For example, the approximated weight percentage (as determined by Eq. ( 3 )) of the most abundant nitrogen-containing compounds (with the elemental composition C c H h N) in the heteroaromatic compound class of all crude oil samples was found to correlate inversely with the API gravity (R 2 > 0.96; Fig. 1 ). The heteroaromatic compound class contains the majority of the C c H h N compounds in every crude oil studied (Fig. 2 ). The structures of the C c H h N compounds in the heteroaromatic compound classes of the five crude oils were further examined. In these compounds, the nitrogen atom can be located either in the aromatic core or outside of it. The location of the nitrogen atoms can be explored by subjecting the ionized compounds to in-source collision-activated dissociation (ISCAD). This method involves acceleration of all ions from the ion source into the ion optics area where they collide with gas molecules. This is a highly energetic dissociation method that can be used to cleave off all alkyl chains from alkyl aromatic ions [23, 24] . Model compound studies demonstrated that ions with different aromatic core sizes and varied alkyl chain lengths all fragment in such a manner that the aromatic core stays intact and some or all of the alkyl side chains are cleaved off (Figs. S2 and S3 ). Therefore, if the nitrogen atom is located outside the aromatic core in the activated ions, it will be lost upon ISCAD. Comparison of the abundances of the C c H h N ions before and after ISCAD shows a substantial decrease in the relative abundances of these ions upon ISCAD for the heavier crude oils but not for the lightest ones (Fig. 3 ).

text: In the last few decades, the average API gravity of crude oil recovered from oil fields has decreased because much of the light crude oil has already been removed. 1 Heavy crude oil reserves account for more than three times the amount of the world reserves of conventional oil and gas combined. 2 The API gravity is defined by the American Petroleum Institute as a measure of the density of the crude oil relative to that of water; 3 the lower the API gravity, the more dense the crude oil. 4 For instance, a study on crude oils processed in the United States showed that the API gravity of crude oils decreased by 0.17 °API/year over a decade. 5 This decline in API gravity has introduced challenges for the transportation, separation, and processing of crude oil, mainly due to the high concentration of asphaltenes. 4 To tackle these challenges, the dilution of heavy crude oil by blending with lighter crude oil and/or condensate oil has been performed to lower the viscosity of the heavy crude oil and thereby improve its mobility during transportation and processing. 6 Condensate oils are liquid hydrocarbon mixtures that are mostly composed of highly volatile and light hydrocarbons. 7 Condensate oils might exist in reservoirs as constituents of natural gas but are recovered as liquids in separators, field facilities, or gas-processing plants. 8 Condensate oils have been shown in some cases to decrease the viscosity of a heavy crude oil more efficiently than light crude oil, 9 likely due to their lower viscosity, and are therefore preferable for dilution of heavy crude oil. The API gravities of condensate oils range between 45 and 75 °API depending on their chemical composition as well as the temperature and the pressure at which they were recovered. 10 Light crude oils have API gravities greater than 31.1 °API. 11 Although condensate oils and light crude oils appear to be good candidates for heavy crude oil dilution, 8 the rheological properties and stability of the diluted crude oil, and, hence, the rate of asphaltene precipitation, depend on the chemical composition of the diluent. 1

metadata.abstract: Although condensate oils are neither well defined nor have a known chemical composition, they are considered by the petroleum industry to be good candidates for the dilution of heavy crude oil as this generates a blend with a lower viscosity. This dilution helps alleviate challenges in heavy crude oil transportation, separation, and processing that are mainly caused by the high concentration of asphaltenes in heavy crude oils. However, asphaltenes in these oil blends are susceptible to precipitation after dilution. Many factors can affect this precipitation, including the amount of polar and heteroaromatic compounds present in the diluent. To facilitate the proper selection of condensate-like oils for heavy crude oil dilution, the chemical compositions of these diluents should be determined. As a proof of concept, five condensate-like oils with different API gravities were analyzed using the previously developed distillation, precipitation, fractionation mass spectrometry method. This method involved fractionation of the samples into five different compound classes (volatile hydrocarbons, heavy saturated hydrocarbons, alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons, heteroaromatic compounds, and polar compounds) and determination of the chemical compositions of compounds in each compound class and in the whole condensate-like oils by using optimized ionization and high-resolution mass spectrometry methods. Further, the average gravimetric weight percentage (wt %) of compounds in each compound class, the average molecular weight, and the average ring and double bond equivalence values of compounds in each class, as well as the overall average molecular weight and ring and double bond equivalence values of the compounds in the entire condensate-like oils, were determined. Additionally, in-source collision-activated dissociation was utilized to determine the average total number of carbon atoms in the alkyl chains of the alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons (ranging from 14 up to 22). Since the API gravity is generally used to make decisions about the quality and price of hydrocarbon products of the petroleum industry, correlations between the API gravity and the chemical compositions of the condensate-like oils were examined. In general, the average wt % of heteroaromatic compounds was greatest in the condensate-like oil with the lowest API gravity (greatest density), while that of saturated hydrocarbons was found to directly correlate with the API gravity. Moreover, consideration of the average wt % of compounds of different elemental composition types in each compound class revealed trends related to the API gravity. text: We have previously developed a method called distillation, precipitation, fractionation mass spectrometry (DPF MS) for the detailed characterization of crude oils. 18, 19 This method involves fractionation of compounds in crude oils into six chemical compound classes, i.e., volatile hydrocarbons, asphaltenes, heavy saturated hydrocarbons, alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons, heteroaromatic compounds, and polar compounds. 18 Each compound class is then analyzed by an optimized mass spectrometric method. In this proof-of-concept study, the types of compounds in five condensate-like oil samples of different API gravities were determined using the DPF MS method. The weight of each compound class was measured, and the gravimetric wt % of each compound class was determined. In addition, the average molecular weight (MW) and ring and double bond equivalence values for compounds in each compound class and in the entire condensate-like oils were determined. Many previous studies that have deployed collisionactivated dissociation (CAD) for the determination of the structures of ionized aromatic compounds in heavy petroleum products have shown that dealkylation is the prevailing fragmentation pathway for ions containing aromatic cores. [20] [21] [22] [23] However, these experiments require prior knowledge of the ions of interest as the ions are isolated and then subjected to CAD. 24 The benefit of in-source CAD (ISCAD) is that it does not require ion isolation as it is applied to all of the ions generated in the ion source. Therefore, ISCAD was utilized in this study to determine the average total number of carbon atoms in the alkyl chains of the compounds in the alkyl aromatic compound class. There have been several previous attempts to find correlations between the bulk physical properties of crude oils and their chemical composition. 19, 25, 26 As API gravity is a major parameter for the classification, quality assessment, and market price assignment of hydrocarbons, 27, 28 correlations found between the API gravity and the chemical compositions of the oil samples are of interest. The samples selected for this study are of interest because they have properties of both condensate oils and light crude oils. They were recovered from fields where condensate oils are recovered and had a condensate oil-like appearance. However, their API gravities were similar to those of light crude oils. From now on, these samples will be referred to as condensate-like oils.

text: The five condensate-like oils of different API gravities were fractionated according to the DPF method 18 into six major compound classes: volatile hydrocarbons, asphaltenes, heavy saturated hydrocarbons, alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons, heteroaromatic compounds, and polar compounds. The first step was vacuum distillation during which the volatile hydrocarbons, including volatile cyclic and naphthenic compounds, typically with boiling points lower than 170 °C, were evaporated, condensed, and collected. The second step was precipitation of the asphaltenes. 30 In this step, n-hexane was added into the sample in a 10:1 ratio after removal of the volatile compounds by distillation. The sample was left undisturbed overnight to precipitate the asphaltenes, if present. 28 After that, the solution was filtered through a 0.45 μm Whatman PTFE membrane filter to collect the asphaltenes. None of the condensate-like oils contained a detectable amount of asphaltenes. The filtrate, referred to as maltenes, was chromatographically fractionated into three compound classes based on their polarity by using a Combi-flash RF 200 auto column system (Teledyne Isco, Inc.) and three different solvents, n-hexane, dichloromethane, and 2-propanol. The n-hexane-eluted fraction contained heavy saturated, cyclic, and alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons, while the dichloromethane and the 2-propanol fractions contained the heteroaromatic and polar compounds, respectively. Finally, the n-hexane-eluted fraction was further subjected to gravitational solid-phase extraction by using a Si/ CN-S-1.5 g solid-phase cartridge (Interchim) to separate the heavy saturated hydrocarbons from the alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons. The mass of each recovered compound class was determined and used in calculating the gravimetric wt % of the class relative to the mass of the sample subjected to fractionation. Sample loss that occurred during transfer and processing was determined after each step and was excluded from the original mass of the analyzed sample. The loss ranged from 10 to 13%, which is similar to those reported in the literature (8-17%). 18, 19 Potential reasons for sample loss during processing include compounds that may not have completely eluted from the auto column system or the solid-phase cartridge with the solvents used. In the future, the DPF method will be improved to reduce sample loss.

text: The chemical classes containing heavy saturated and cyclic hydrocarbons (i.e., those alkanes that could not be separated by vacuum distillation), alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons, heteroaromatic compounds, and polar compounds were analyzed using a Thermo Scientific LQIT/orbitrap MS coupled to an atmospheric pressure chemical ionization (APCI) source as previously described. 18 All analyses were performed in the positive ion mode. For the chemical class containing heavy saturated and cyclic hydrocarbons, n-hexane was used as the solvent and APCI reagent, while oxygen was employed in place of nitrogen as the sheath and auxiliary gas ((+)APCI/O 2 /nhexane). These conditions are known to predominantly produce [M -H] + ions. 31 For the chemical classes containing alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons and heteroaromatic compounds, CS 2 was used as the solvent and APCI reagent, while nitrogen was used as the sheath and auxiliary gas ((+)APCI/N 2 /CS 2 ). These conditions mostly produce stable molecular ions [M +• ]. Polar compounds were ionized in the APCI source by using a 3:1 methanol/n-hexane solution as the solvent/ reagent and N 2 as the sheath and auxiliary gas ((+)APCI/N 2 /3:1 methanol/n-hexane). This approach predominantly generates stable [M + H] + ions for these analytes. These previously reported, optimal APCI conditions for each compound class were used to achieve optimum ionization without substantial fragmentation. 18 Each sample was diluted in the appropriate solvent to obtain a concentration of 30 mg mL -1 , and this solution was directly injected into the APCI source by using a 500 μL syringe at the flow rates of 10, 3, 3, and 1 μL min -1 for the saturated hydrocarbons, alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons, heteroaromatic compounds, and polar compound classes, respectively, as was previously reported. 18 All ions were transferred into the orbitrap for high-resolution analysis (100 000 resolution at m/z 400). Twenty microscans were collected to obtain each mass spectrum. Mass calibration and tuning were conducted on a regular basis by using a Pierce LTQ ESI positive ion calibration solution (covers m/z range 150-2000; obtained from Thermo Scientific) and Agilent LC/MS tuning mix for APCI (covers m/z range 50-2000). The mass accuracies of the calibration agents are provided in Table S2A and Figure S1A .

text: The distillates containing the volatile hydrocarbons were analyzed using a LECO Pegasus 4D GC × GC/(EI)TOF instrument equipped with an Agilent 7890B twodimensional gas chromatograph (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA) by using a method described previously. 19 In detail, the volatile hydrocarbons were dissolved at a concentration of 1.0 wt/wt % in highpurity n-pentane (>99%). An auto injector (Agilent G4513A) was used to inject 0.5 μL of the solutions into a split/splitless injector with a split ratio of 1:20 that was held at 260 °C under a constant flow of helium carrier gas (1.25 mL min -1 ). text: Compound Classes of the Five Condensate-like Oils. The average gravimetric wt % of compounds in each compound class was determined from the mass of compounds in each class relative to the mass of the sample subjected to fractionation. Each fractionation experiment was carried out twice, and the results were highly reproducible (data, averages, standard deviations (SDs), and confidence intervals are provided in Table S3 in the Supporting Information (SI)). For all standard deviation measurements in this study, the data were assumed to be normally distributed. Since the mean values provided for all measurements in this study are an estimate of the population mean, we provided the 95% confidence interval of the mean at α = 0.05. 35, 36 When considering the average gravimetric wt % of different types of compounds in all five condensate-like oils, heavy saturated hydrocarbons corresponded to the majority of the compounds (Table 1 ; 81.0% in the lightest condensate-like oil (with the greatest API gravity) vs 69.9% in the heaviest condensate-like oil (with the lowest API gravity)), followed by alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons (Table 1 ; 6.9% in the lightest condensate-like oil vs 10.3% in the heaviest condensate-like oil). The gravimetric wt % of compounds in the volatile hydrocarbon, heteroaromatic compound, and polar compound classes was each found to be less than 4.0%. Similarly, in a previous study on light crude oils, the greatest gravimetric wt % was found for the heavy saturated hydrocarbons (44.3-48.2%) followed by alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons (17.5-21.2%), while the volatile saturated hydrocarbons, heteroaromatic compounds, and polar compounds all had wt % lower than 10.0%. 19 Plots of the gravimetric wt % of compounds in each compound class in the five condensate-like oils as a function of their API gravities are shown in Figure 1 and the SI. Linear correlations were only found for the heteroaromatic compound and the heavy saturated hydrocarbon classes (Figure 1 ). The heavier condensate-like oils with smaller API gravities contain more heteroaromatic compounds (R 2 = 1.00; Figure 1A ) and less heavy saturated hydrocarbons (R 2 = 0.94; Figure 1B ) than the lighter condensate-like oils with a greater API gravity. A similar correlation between the API gravity and gravimetric wt % of heteroaromatic compounds in heavy, medium, and light crude oils has been previously reported. 19

text: Compound Classes. The average MW of compounds in hydrocarbon oils is thought to determine many of their physical properties, including the API gravity and viscosity. 40 Petroleum industries typically determine the average MW values by using freezing point depression, GC-simulated distillation techniques, or gel permeation chromatography. 18, [41] [42] [43] [44] However, a previous study on model compound mixtures showed that the average MW values determined by using freezing point depression or GC-simulated distillation techniques were underestimated, 18 while that obtained using the DPF MS method was accurate (for these model compound mixtures). The average MWs of the compounds in the whole condensate-like oils ranged between 253 and 327 Da (data from two experiments on each compound class; the individual measured values, their averages, and standard deviations are shown in Table S11 ). On the other hand, the average MWs determined previously for compounds in condensate-like oils (API gravity not provided) by using gel permeation chromatography were lower, ranging from 228 to 243 Da. 44 It has been previously reported that the gel permeation method does not provide accurate average MW values for heavy petroleum compounds, partially due to complications in the elution behavior caused by intramolecular hydrogen bonding and due to lack of suitable reference compounds. 45, 46 Indeed, the measured values are usually associated with large errors (>10%) 47 compared to a typical error of <3% for the values determined by the DPF MS method. 18 Therefore, the values obtained here using the DPF MS method are likely to be more accurate. The average MWs of the compounds in all of the condensatelike oils (ranging from 253 to 327 Da) are lower than that (473 Da) of a medium-light crude oil (31.14 °API) previously determined by using the DPF MS method. 18 This crude oil was denser than the condensate-like oil samples studied here, in agreement with the determined average MWs. Heavy crude oils tend to contain many large compounds, such as asphaltenes and resins. 2 The lower average MWs of compounds in the condensate-like oils may be attributed to the smaller amounts of large compounds, i.e., asphaltenes and large polar compounds, 48 in the condensate-like oils.

text: As a proof of concept, the chemical compositions of five condensate-like oils of different API gravities were determined by using the DPF MS methodology. No measurable amounts of asphaltenes were found in any of the tested condensate-like oils. Since the viscosity of crude oils is largely determined by their asphaltene content, 51 this explains the greater API gravity of these condensate-like oils compared to that of heavier crude oils. 3 The absence of asphaltenes makes these condensate-like oils good candidates for diluting heavy crude oils. However, other factors may also affect the dissolution of asphaltenes in crude oil blends, including the amount of polar and heteroaromatic compounds. Based on the gravimetric percentages determined for the five compound classes obtained using the DPF method (volatile hydrocarbons, heavy saturated hydrocarbons, alkyl aromatic hydrocarbons, heteroaromatic compounds, and polar compounds) for each condensate-like oil, correlations with the API gravity were found only for the wt % of the heteroaromatic compound and the heavy saturated hydrocarbon classes in the five oils. The wt % of heteroaromatic compounds was found to be inversely related with the API gravity, while the wt % of the saturated hydrocarbons was found to directly correlate with the API gravity. Similar results were previously reported for crude oils of different API gravities. 52 Examination of the elemental composition types of compounds in the condensate-like oils and determination of their wt % by using high-resolution mass spectrometry revealed that compounds with the elemental composition type C c H h were generally the most abundant compounds in the condensate-like oils, with an approximate wt % between 57 and 77%. Examination of the molecular composition types of compounds in the individual compound classes in each condensate-like oil provided more information. For example, the heaviest condensate-like oil 1(37.50 °API) contained more compounds with the elemental composition types C c H h S s and C c H h N n O o S s than the lighter condensate-like oils. However, no correlations were found between the API gravity and the average wt % of compounds with the elemental composition types C c H h N n , C c H h O o , C c H h O o S s , C c H h N n O o , and C c H h N n O o S s .

text: Due to the ever-increasing energy demand, the world's light crude oil reserves are diminishing. 1 In order to recover approximately 66% of crude oil that still remains in underground reservoirs after primary and secondary oil recovery processes, novel extraction methods must be developed. 1 One of the most intriguing tertiary recovery methods is chemically enhanced oil recovery (cEOR). 2 The goal of this process is to mobilize oil bound in the reservoir by introducing a combination of salts, surfactants, and polymers into the water flooding solution. 3 The salts and surfactants are selected to decrease the interfacial tension of the oil bound to the reservoir surface, while the polymers increase the viscosity of the injected water and thereby facilitate the motion of the displaced oil. 3 However, petroleum companies rarely invest in cEOR efforts due to the insufficient levels of oil recovered compared to the amount of money spent on developing cEOR approaches. 2 An improved understanding of the types of compounds in oil that bind tightly to the reservoir surface would facilitate the development of more successful cEOR formulations, that is, optimal salt/surfactant/polymer mixtures, for more efficient extraction of the oil from the ground. While oil reservoirs can have numerous mineral surfaces, the presence of clay minerals in the rock is believed to play a dominant role in binding oil constituents because of their expansive specific surface areas. 4 One of the most abundant clay minerals in oil reservoirs is kaolinite. 4 It has been extensively studied due to its high affinity for crude oil. 5 Kaolinite is an aluminosilicate with the chemical composition Al 2 Si 2 O 5 (OH) 4 . It is a layered mineral with one sheet of silica tetrahedrons (SiO 4 ) connected via oxygen atoms to a sheet of alumina octahedrons [Al 2 O(H) 6 ]. The exposed OH groups on the alumina octahedral layer of kaolinite are thought to create favorable interactions between the clay and the most polar compounds present in crude oil, especially the polar compounds in asphaltenes. [6] [7] [8] On the other hand, the siloxane surface of kaolinite has been reported to have favorable interactions with the most nonpolar compounds in crude oil. 9

metadata.abstract: Chemically enhanced oil recovery (cEOR) is an expensive endeavor that yields modest levels of oil recovery. In order to make it economically viable, an improved understanding of the process is needed. For example, knowledge of the types of compounds in crude oil that are strongly bound to reservoir surfaces would facilitate the design of more efficient cEOR formulations. In this research study, the fractionation step of the previously published distillation, precipitation, and fractionation mass spectrometry (MS) method was utilized to determine the types of compounds in crude oil that are strongly or weakly bound to kaolinite, a prevalent clay mineral found in many oil reservoirs. The results obtained using high-resolution MS experiments revealed that the average molecular weight and the number of aromatic rings were similar for both the strongly and weakly bound compounds. On the other hand, hydrocarbons with no heteroatoms were ∼2.5 times more abundant in the strongly bound compounds than in the nonbound compounds, while heteroatom-containing compounds were more abundant in the nonbound compounds. An analogous binding study performed on a model compound mixture corroborated the above findings that nonpolar compounds prefer to bind to kaolinite than polar compounds. These results suggest that more valuable oil components (nonpolar hydrocarbons) remain in the reservoirs after water flooding, and therefore, cEOR efforts with the appropriate formulation could increase the economic feasibility of the process. [29] [30] [31] [32] [33] [34] [35] The affinity that kaolinite can have for both polar and nonpolar compounds makes it challenging to develop a successful combination of chemicals for cEOR and release the bound oil. Therefore, a better understanding of which particular compounds in crude oil bind strongly to kaolinite could accelerate the development of better cEOR formulations. While many efforts have been made to computationally model the adsorption of compounds present in crude oil to kaolinite, [10] [11] [12] [13] [14] [15] only a few experimental studies have been conducted. Two independent studies determined positive correlations between the nitrogen content in asphaltene samples and the amount of asphaltenes adsorbed to kaolinite. 7, 16 On the contrary, based on X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy profile measurements of asphaltenes adsorbed to kaolinite surfaces, nitrogen-and sulfur-rich asphaltenes were demonstrated not to be strongly adsorbed to kaolinite. 8 However, the analytical techniques utilized in the above studies provided only bulk chemical information for the compounds strongly bound to kaolinite and provided no molecular-level information. At this time, no experimental studies have been performed to determine the types of compounds in whole crude oil, and not just in asphaltenes, that strongly bind to kaolinite. This is the goal of the present work. Various high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry (MS) experiments have been critical in obtaining molecular-level information for crude oil and asphaltenes, including the average molecular weight (AvgMW) of the compounds in these mixtures and the elemental compositions and the number of aromatic rings in individual compounds. text: [24] [25] Recently, our research group developed an improved method for fractionating and characterizing compounds in crude oil called distillation, precipitation, and fractionation MS (DPF MS). [20] [21] [22] In the aforementioned study, optimized mass spectrometric ionization methods were developed for each fraction to minimize ionization biases within the fraction and the extent of fragmentation of the generated ions. [20] [21] [22] These measurements yield semiquantitative information on the weight percentages of the different compounds. [20] [21] [22] The fractionation part of the DPF MS method 20, 21 was utilized in this research study to better understand the types of compounds in crude oil that bind strongly to mineral surfaces. text: A medium API gravity crude oil (31.0°API gravity) sample was provided by Neste Corporation. The crude oil was stored in amber glass bottles to minimize oxidation, and the containers were tightly sealed to minimize the evaporation of volatile compounds. The containers were stored in a freezer at -20 °C. Kaolinite used in this study was the well-crystalline KGa-1b kaolinite obtained from Source Clays Repository from The Clay Minerals Society. 28 Fluorene (98% purity), dibenzothiophene (98%), dibenzofuran (96%), carbazole (>99%), and 1-heptadecylbenzene (>97%), the compounds used in the model compound mixture, were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO) and used as received. CS 2 (99.9 %) was purchased from Alfa Aesar (Haverhill, MA). Methanol [Optima; liquid chromatography (LC)/MS grade] was purchased from Fisher Scientific (Hampton, NH). High-performance LC (HPLC) grade nhexane, dichloromethane (DCM), isopropanol (IPA), and toluene were purchased from Fisher Chemical (West Lafayette, IN) and used as received. A synthetic brine solution was made to match that used in the targeted cEOR reservoir. In this case, the solution contained 8960 mg/ L total dissolved solids with sodium cations being the dominant cation (3490 mg/L) and chloride and bicarbonate anions being the dominant anions with concentrations of 4460 and 774 mg/L, respectively. 2.2. Exposure of the Model Compound Mixture and Crude Oil to Kaolinite. Kaolinite was exposed to crude oil by combining 9.0 g of crude oil with 6.0 g of kaolinite clay (1.5 g of crude oil/g of kaolinite) in a Corex tube. Similarly, in a separate Corex tube, a 0.02 M equimolar solution of fluorene (C 13 H 10 ), dibenzothiophene (C 12 H 8 S), dibenzofuran (C 12 H 8 O), and carbazole (C 12 H 9 N) was prepared in 6 mL of toluene (see Figure 1 for the structures of the compounds). Toluene was selected as the solvent because it dissolved all compounds. The entire solution was mixed with 4.0 g of dried, powdered kaolinite clay in a Corex centrifuge tube. Each sample described above was thoroughly mixed using a rotatory mixer at 50 RPM for 7 days. The mixtures were then shaken by hand, followed by centrifugation for 30 min at 3000 RPM.

Each fraction was weighed gravimetrically to obtain the weight percent of crude oil compounds in the NBC and KBC samples. It should be noted here that it is highly unlikely that this treatment only removes the top monolayer of the material from kaolinite. Hence, we assume that several monolayers were removed. After evaporating the solvents from the three fractions, DCM was added into each fraction, and then the fractions were combined before analysis. On the other hand, the toluene solvent of the mixture containing the NBC of the model compound mixture was evaporated, and the sample was fractionated as discussed above for the crude oil. The fractions were dissolved in DCM and combined for gas chromatography/electron ionization MS(GC/EI MS) analysis of the relative abundance of the four model compounds in a single analysis. 2.4.

TGA of Kaolinite Samples Exposed to Crude Oil. 0.04-0.06 g of the kaolinite samples (kaolinite exposed to crude oil; kaolinite exposed to crude oil after n-hexane extraction; kaolinite exposed to crude oil after n-hexane and DCM extractions; and kaolinite exposed to crude oil after n-hexane, DCM, and IPA extractions) were analyzed using a Mettler Toledo TGA Sdta851 thermogravimetric analyzer. The initial temperature was set to 25 °C, and the temperature was increased at a rate of 20 °C/min until it reached a final temperature of 1000 °C under the flow of N 2 gas. For the kaolinite-crude oil complexes, any mass loss above this value is due to the loss of crude oil compounds bound to the kaolinite surface. TGA measurements were only conducted on kaolinite exposed to the crude oil and not on kaolinite exposed to the model compound mixture.

All FTIR spectra were collected using a liquid N 2 -cooled HgCdTe (MCT) detector. FTIR measurements were only conducted on the crude oil sample and not on the model compound mixture. 2.6. GC/EI MS for the Analysis of KBCs and NBCs in the Model Compound Mixture. Toluene in the solution containing NBCs and the three flash column fractions containing KBCs of the model compound mixture was evaporated. 1.0 mg of the KBC sample and 1.0 mg of the NBC sample were each dissolved in 1 mL of DCM prior to analysis using a Shimadzu GC-2010/MS-QP2010 GC/MS instrument. All high-resolution measurements were performed at a resolution of 100,000 at m/z 400. text: The goal of this work was to identify the types of compounds in crude oil that most strongly bind to kaolinite (KBC) (a nonswelling clay) by using a modified DPF MS method. Finally, to better understand the results of this study, a 0.02 mM equimolar model compound mixture containing fluorene, dibenzothiophene, dibenzofuran, and carbazole was exposed to kaolinite using the same method as that used for the crude oil (see "Exposure of the Model Compound Mixture and Crude Oil to Kaolinite" in the Experimental Section for details), and the KBC fractions were analyzed as described above. The model compounds that were strongly bound and not strongly bound to kaolinite were identified and quantified using GC/EI MS. The results are discussed below in this order.

text: Additional kaolinite adsorption tests were conducted with a four-compound model compound mixture to corroborate the above finding that nonpolar hydrocarbons bind to kaolinite more strongly than heteroatom-containing compounds. The experiments were performed in a similar manner to those for the crude oil, but the final flash chromatography fractions obtained for NBCs and KBCs were combined before analysis. Figure 8 shows a bar graph of the relative GC peak areas for each of the four model compounds in each sample -NBCs (blue) and KBCs (orange). Error bars represent the standard deviations of three replicate measurements collected on three different days. In agreement with the previous results, the most nonpolar compound (fluorene) was found on an average to have a greater relative abundance in the KBC sample (∼30%) than in the NBC sample (∼25%), while the nitrogen-and oxygen-containing compounds had substantially greater relative abundances in the NBC sample (∼21 and ∼24%, respectively) than in the KBC sample (∼13 and ∼18%, respectively). These findings support the conclusion made in the crude oil study that nonpolar hydrocarbons are more strongly bound to kaolinite than nitrogen-and oxygencontaining compounds. Furthermore, greater amounts of the sulfur-containing compound (dibenzothiophene) were found to be present in the KBC sample than in the NBC sample. Based on these results, nonpolar hydrocarbons have a higher affinity for kaolinite than polar compounds. Although the relatively nonpolar sulfur-containing compounds derived from the crude oil had greater abundances in the NBC sample than in the KBC sample, this is rationalized based on the fact that crude oil contains many different sulfur-compounds with different structures and not just dibenzothiophene used in the model compound mixture. Therefore, different sulfur-containing model compounds need to be studied in the future.

text: Examination of the types of compounds in crude oil that are strongly or weakly bound to kaolinite, a prevalent clay mineral in oil reservoirs, revealed that many properties of the compounds that were found to bind strongly to kaolinite were similar to those of the nonbound compounds. For example, the AvgMWs of the compounds in the heavy, saturated, and alkylaromatic compound fractions, heteroaromatic compound fractions, and polar compound fractions were similar for both samples. Also, the average RDBE values were similar between the corresponding fractions for both samples, with the exception of the polar compound fraction for which the RDBE was much greater for KBCs (7) than for NBCs (3). Nonpolar hydrocarbons in the crude oil were found to bind more strongly to kaolinite than polar compounds containing heteroatoms. The results obtained in a model compound study corroborated this finding. They also demonstrated that nonpolar hydrocarbons bind strongly to kaolinite. Therefore, cEOR efforts to improve crude oil recovery may be possible if surfactants and polymers are designed to target the nonpolar hydrocarbons present in crude oil. Furthermore, the results from this study suggest that the more useful and more valuable oil components (compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen atoms), with the exception of the sulfur-containing compounds, preferentially remain in the ground after water flooding, and therefore, cEOR efforts with the appropriate formulation could be economically favorable. The procedure developed here for exposing crude oil to kaolinite as well as the procedure developed for recovering the bound oil compounds can be applied to other types of clay minerals. Furthermore, in combination with high-resolution MS for chemical analysis, the chemical composition of oil components that bind strongly to different types of clay minerals can be studied and the influence of changes in pH, salinity, and temperature will be explored in the future to determine whether these variables change the type of compounds in the crude oil that bind to kaolinite.
